newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares, dollar fall on interest rate news.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares, dollar fall on interest rate news.

text.p: Tel Aviv shares opened down on Tuesday, reflecting disappointment in a Bank of Israel decision not to lower interest rates in December, traders said.
On the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares fell in early trading by 1.03 percent, or 2.02 points, to 194.77.
The dollar weakened against the shekel despite flexing its muscles elsewhere in the world, falling to 3.2394 against the shekel compared with 3.2470 at closing on Monday.
Israel's business sector says the central bank's firm monetary policy artificially boosts the shekel and hurts exports.
"Companies are suffering from the low exchange rate," said Danny Alt, head of portfolios at Nesuah Trading and Investment.
"And the Mishtanim is down about one percent because of the disappointment in the interest rate," he added.
The Bank of Israel announced on Monday, after the stock market closed, that its key lending rate would stay at an annualised 15.2 percent in December.
But one trader said the news that Bank Governor Jacob Frenkel was standing firm was not at all bad for foreign investors, who hold about 10 percent of the shares on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

"All in all I would say for foreign investors such an announcement should be viewed as a positive one because it looks as if there is somebody standing alone and fighting against inflation," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Zannex Securities.
The central bank, concerned with inflation running at 11 percent a year, says it cannot ease up on monetary policy until the government makes a substantial effort to slash spending.

"I would say that for the time being the reaction of the market seems to be much better than it could have been," Nahum said. "And I won't be surprised if the market will return to a positive trend within a few days, maybe even tomorrow and maybe even today."
Lawmakers are haggling over government proposals, due to be passed on December 31, to slash between 4.9 billion and 6.9 billion shekels from the 1997 spending package.
